lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop a much deeper understanding of pronouns and how they work alongside nouns. The lesson moves beyond simply spotting pronouns: students learn why writers use them, how different types of pronoun function, and how careful pronoun choices can make writing clearer and less repetitive.

This lesson includes:
✔ Revising common, proper, countable and non-countable nouns
✔ Understanding how pronouns replace nouns and reduce unnecessary repetition
✔ Recognising personal, possessive, relative, reflexive, demonstrative, interrogative and indefinite pronouns
✔ Distinguishing personal pronouns from possessive pronouns
✔ Choosing pronouns that make sense in context and show ownership correctly
✔ Balancing nouns and pronouns so writing remains clear rather than confusing
✔ Identifying the noun or noun phrase to which a pronoun refers
✔ Using pronouns to improve the fluency and cohesion of writing

Students first revisit different types of noun before seeing how pronouns can replace repeated nouns. They then compare personal and possessive pronouns, explore a wider range of pronoun types, sort and identify pronouns in sentences, and practise choosing suitable pronouns for gaps and their own sentences. A key focus is clarity: students see that overusing pronouns can make a paragraph confusing if the reader cannot tell which noun a pronoun refers to.

By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to identify several types of pronoun, choose pronouns accurately, link them back to the correct noun or noun phrase, and use nouns and pronouns together to improve the fluency and cohesion of their writing.

In this lesson, students build verbal reasoning skills by analysing how words are formed, related, pronounced and used. The lesson combines vocabulary knowledge with logic and pattern spotting, so students have to explain connections rather than rely on recall alone.

This lesson includes:
✔ Building verbal comprehension, logic and word-based problem-solving skills
✔ Recognising relationships between words, including opposites, categories and analogies
✔ Identifying odd-one-out words using meaning, spelling or pronunciation
✔ Working with palindromes, compound words and letter patterns
✔ Finding hidden words across neighbouring words
✔ Rearranging letters and words to solve anagrams and sentence problems
✔ Applying word codes and missing-letter rules
✔ Using careful vocabulary knowledge to infer the best answer from context

Students work through a broad range of verbal reasoning question types, including word relationships, opposites, odd-one-out questions, hidden words, palindromes, compound words, letter patterns, word codes and rearrangement tasks. They also use context and grammatical relationships to decide which answer best fits a question. The activities progressively require closer attention to spelling, meaning, sound and structure.

By the end of the lesson, learners should be more confident at recognising verbal patterns, making precise word connections and applying a systematic approach to unfamiliar verbal reasoning questions.

Students move between representations and numerical reasoning so that the underlying number relationships are understood rather than memorised as isolated rules. They practise selecting the relevant place-value information, applying the correct rule and checking whether their answers are sensible.
